recorded: Late 1953 or January 1954, Salle Adyar, Paris
intro: Couperin’s Les Barricades mystérieuses is a low-lying harpsichord piece in four voices, in which one note is held over while the next chord begins. Marcelle Meyer plays it on the piano.

sections.label: A · Refrain in B♭ major
sections.mNote: Four voices enter at different moments in B♭ major.

sections.label: B · Two couplets and their refrains
sections.mNote: Short episodes lead back to the opening tune.

sections.label: C · Third couplet, longer
sections.mNote: The bass moves farther beneath the tied notes.

sections.label: A′ · Refrain returns in B♭
sections.mNote: The refrain’s voices close together on B♭.

cues.title: Four voices in the bass clef
cues.text: Couperin writes four voices in a low register, with both staves in the bass clef. Their notes overlap, as ties carry one voice into the next chord while another begins a new figure. The marking is Vivement, lively.
cues.evidence: Score, refrain, bars 1–9; Les Éditions Outremontaises (2004). https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP128589-WIMA.0099-Couperin_6eOrdre_Les_Baricades.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wigmore Hall recital, 1927
cues.text: At Wigmore Hall on 11 May 1927, Meyer played Les Barricades mystérieuses on a programme that also included Ravel’s Jeux d’eau and Stravinsky’s Piano-Rag-Music. She kept Couperin in her repertoire for decades. This recording comes from her Paris sessions of 1953–54.
cues.evidence: Meyer chronology, 11 May 1927 programme and 1953–54 Salle Adyar sessions, Les Discophiles Français DF 86. https://classical-pianists.net/viii/marcelle-meyer/chronology/

cues.title: Third couplet
cues.text: The third couplet, bars 31–53, is longer than either of the first two. The bass keeps moving beneath the overlapping voices, and extra flats appear in the chords. At its end Couperin writes Rondeau again, and the opening refrain returns.
cues.evidence: Score, third couplet and Rondeau direction, bars 31–53. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP128589-WIMA.0099-Couperin_6eOrdre_Les_Baricades.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: First couplet over a B♭ bass
transitions.to: B · Two couplets and their refrains
transitions.how: The first couplet (bars 11–22) follows the repeated refrain and begins over B♭ in the bass. The upper voices reach higher notes. Couperin keeps the staggered entries and ties of the refrain, and the two-beat motion continues. Meyer’s two hands still carry all four voices. The marking remains Vivement.
transitions.evidence: Score, first couplet after the repeated refrain, bars 11–22. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP128589-WIMA.0099-Couperin_6eOrdre_Les_Baricades.pdf

transitions.title: The bass descends from B♭
transitions.from: B · Two couplets and their refrains
transitions.how: The third couplet (bars 31–52) follows the B♭ major refrain with no break in its chain of tied notes. The bass descends, and the upper voices go on entering between the beats. More flats appear as the passage continues. Couperin keeps the marking Vivement and the two-beat metre, and this final episode runs to more bars than the earlier couplets.
transitions.evidence: Score, third couplet, bars 31–52, especially its descending bass at the opening. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP128589-WIMA.0099-Couperin_6eOrdre_Les_Baricades.pdf

transitions.title: The refrain and its final chord
transitions.how: The bass reaches F, and the written Rondeau then sends the pianist back to the B♭ major refrain. The refrain’s interlocking notes return unchanged. In the final ending, marked Fin, a single held B♭ major chord takes the place of their overlapping movement.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 52–53 and the final ending marked Fin after the refrain. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP128589-WIMA.0099-Couperin_6eOrdre_Les_Baricades.pdf

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Commons identifies Meyer; the pianist’s recording chronology identifies the Couperin programme. This is a piano performance, notwithstanding the source category for harpsichord music.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Solo piano performance of the harpsichord rondeau
fields.note: The nominated file contains the individual character piece, not the complete sixth ordre. The work was published in the 1717 second book. Meyer’s performing edition and every repeat choice are unestablished; the inspected modern score is an analytical reference, not an attribution of her edition. No uncut claim is made from duration alone.

fields.note: This uncertainty is stated in the Commons Author field. The recording chronology gives the broader 1953/1954 range. No single year or session day has been selected. 23 September 2023 is the Commons upload date, not the session; the filename’s 1954 does not resolve the range.

composer.epithet: Musician who played for Louis XIV on Sundays, known at the harpsichord for held notes, trills and well-placed silences.
facts: Son of Charles Couperin; nephew of Louis; organist at Saint-Gervais from 1685
Royal chapel organist from 1693; chamber harpsichordist from 1717
Four books, 1713–30: 27 ordres; L’Art de toucher le clavecin, 1716–17
Two organ masses; Leçons de Ténèbres; chamber concerts and viol suites
composer.background:
On Sundays in 1714 and 1715, François Couperin played chamber music for the ageing Louis XIV. The violinist François Duval joined him, with wind players and a viol; Couperin played the harpsichord. When he published the Concerts royaux in 1722, he recalled that the king had summoned him “almost every Sunday of the year”. The dances in the collection, among them an allemande, a grave sarabande and a little chaconne, had been played in the king’s rooms. Louis XIV had once danced in his own court ballets.

Couperin was born in Paris in 1668, into a family already established at the organ of Saint-Gervais. His uncle Louis had held the post before his father Charles, and had died before François was born. When Charles died in 1679, the church kept the succession open for the boy, and Michel-Richard de Lalande covered the duties until he was ready. François studied with Jacques Thomelin and took over in 1685. At twenty-five he won one of the four organists’ places at the royal chapel. He kept his Paris work, travelled to court for his quarter of service and taught the royal children.
